newsitem.title: HONG KONG: BA chief defends American alliance plan.
newsitem.headline: BA chief defends American alliance plan.

text.p: The chief executive of British Airways (BA) defended on Wednesday the airline's proposed alliance with American Airlines which has been criticised by rival airlines as an effort to block competition.
"I unconditionally reject...the suggestion that British Airways is not willing to be competitive," chief executive Robert Ayling said at a news conference in Hong Kong.
"British Airways has, above all airlines, been willing to compete freely in liberal, open markets," he said.

The proposed alliance has attracted fierce criticism from Virgin and several U.S. airlines including BA's estranged U.S. eastcoast partner US Air, as well as some consumer groups, who say the alliance will dominate the trans-Atlantic market.
Under the plan, BA will coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
They also intend to combine their frequent flyer programmes and share flight booking codes to promote their connecting flights on computer reservation systems.
"The industry is becoming globalised...the nature of competition in international aviation is increasingly between the alliances and across the different hubs or connecting points," Ayling said.
Both airlines were now waiting for a ruling from the British Monopolies and Mergers Commission, Ayling said.
BA, like other airlines, have been hit by rising jet fuel costs this year, Ayling said.

"They are 25 percent higher this year than they were this time last year...it's an additional cost which we will have to find some way of carrying and it's more than I was expecting at the beginning of this year," he said.
Jet fuel prices, which has risen continuously since June, now stand at US$29.95 per barrel, free-on-board in Singapore. It stood at US$22.65 per barrel this time last year.
